Do safe spaces and trigger warnings weaken us?
Nope, not at all... I cannot even keep this shit going. Yes, it hurts us.

So with some experience in trauma recovery, 100% it's bad for us with how it's being shoved down our throats. There's nothing wrong with a women's shelter or a men's shelter for persons to go to escape violence. Those are supposed to be safe spaces, they offer people safety from physical harm. However trying to make a place safe from things like ideas is stupid and sad, especially when people want to wave the flag of hurt feelings and trauma. In trauma recovery, you're taught some very simple things and the most important 2 are to not avoid things because they might trigger you, and confront the hell out of the events that actually happened to you.

I came back from deployment all fuckered up, and I've been in treatment since early 2010 for PTSD and a slew of other problems(bombs suck). With all those years of treatment there are 2 things that have been the most beneficial to myself, and other recovering veterans and civilians across the board. Cognitive Processing Therapy(CPT) and Prolonged Exposure(PE).

In CPT you confront your symptoms and their sources, identify them, and work on methods of bringing your distress down from scenarios that trigger them to regain a more normal ability to regulate yourself emotionally. It's hard to stare that shit in the face, but you get better for it. You. Get. Better.

In PE you go way deeper than you do in CPT. You're spending two hours a week with a therapist being forced to tell and relive an event over and over and over and over and over again. When you leave that office you have homework. You have to write that event over and over and over and over and over again. You listen to recordings of yourself in session every day. You have to go out and confront things that trigger you. You have to go out and challenge yourself daily. For months. It's hard as fuck. It's brutal as fuck because you're relieving the most painful and horrific moments of your entire life, but again: You. Get. Fucking. Better.

It's hard. Oh darn. You're damn right it's hard. You get PTSD because something fucking horrific happens and you don't get over that by hiding under a blanket and pretending it didn't happen. That's called avoidance and avoidance is the strongest reinforcing tool you can ever have for making your trauma worse. Of course, you would have to have experienced an actual traumatic event so severe that it reprograms the way your brain is wired and firing to have PTSD in the first place.
